thread.title: Average car payments and auto loan debt continue to rise in 2026, report shows
thread.title_full: Average car payments and auto loan debt continue to rise in 2026, report shows

author: d. m. priest
title: Average car payments and auto loan debt continue to rise in 2026, report shows
text:
The average monthly payment for a new car reached $767 in the fourth quarter of 2025, an increase of 2.8% from the same period a year earlier, according to data released by LendingTree on Mar. 26. Payments for used and leased vehicles also rose by 1.7% and 1.5%, respectively.
These increases reflect ongoing trends in vehicle pricing and borrowing habits across the United States. The report indicates that Americans are borrowing more for both new and used cars, with average loan amounts at $43,582 for new vehicles and $27,528 for used ones.
Auto loan debt remains the second-largest category of consumer debt after mortgages. As of Q4 2025, Americans owe a total of $1.667 trillion in auto loans, accounting for about 8.9% of all consumer debt nationwide.
Delinquency rates have also risen slightly; the percentage of outstanding auto loans at least 90 days overdue was reported at 5.2% in Q4 2025—close to its previous peak recorded in late 2010—while shorter-term delinquencies saw a slight decrease compared to last year.
LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst Matt Schulz said: “That’s such a long time to be stuck paying for a depreciating asset… However, once that initial glow wears off and you’re still making a big monthly payment on that vehicle after five-plus years, it may not seem worth it.” Schulz also cautioned against high-interest “buy-here, pay-here” financing options often available to consumers with lower credit scores: “Not only can the sticker price be bigger, but the interest rates can look more like credit card rates than typical auto loan rates… In short, these should be among the last options you’d consider.”
Banks currently hold the largest share of auto financing at nearly one-third of all loans (31.8%), followed by credit unions (22.2%) and captive lenders associated with manufacturers (19.3%). Borrowers with higher credit scores continue to secure larger loans on average than those with lower scores.
Schulz encouraged consumers to shop around when seeking an auto loan: “Good credit means more good options… Once you’ve found a deal you’re happy with, get preapproved by the lender.”
As prices remain high and terms stretch longer than ever before—often approaching six years—the impact on household budgets is likely to persist through coming quarters.

These increases reflect ongoing trends in vehicle pricing and borrowing habits across the United States. As of Q4 2025, Americans owe a total of $1.667 trillion in auto loans, accounting for about 8.9% of all consumer debt nationwide.
